import Mathlib

inductive BinarySearchTree : Type
| Empty : BinarySearchTree
| Node : Int → BinarySearchTree → BinarySearchTree → BinarySearchTree

def view (t : BinarySearchTree) : Set Int :=
  match t with
  | BinarySearchTree.Empty => ∅
  | BinarySearchTree.Node v l r => view l ∪ view r ∪ {v}

def is_bst (t : BinarySearchTree) : Prop :=
  match t with
  | BinarySearchTree.Empty => True
  | BinarySearchTree.Node v l r =>
    (∀ x ∈ view l, x < v) ∧
    is_bst l ∧
    (∀ x ∈ view r, x > v) ∧
    is_bst r

-- Precondition definitions
@[reducible, simp]
def search_precond (t : BinarySearchTree) (v : Int) : Prop :=
  -- !benchmark @start precond
  is_bst t
  -- !benchmark @end precond

-- !benchmark @start auxcode
def searchAux : BinarySearchTree → Int → Bool
  | BinarySearchTree.Empty, _ => false
  | BinarySearchTree.Node x l r, v =>
      if v = x then true
      else if v < x then searchAux l v
      else searchAux r v
-- !benchmark @end auxcode

-- Main function definition
def search (t : BinarySearchTree) (v : Int)
    (h_precond : search_precond t v) : Bool :=
  -- !benchmark @start code
  searchAux t v
  -- !benchmark @end code

-- Postcondition definitions
@[reducible, simp]
def search_postcond (t : BinarySearchTree) (v : Int) (result : Bool)
    (_ : search_precond t v) : Prop :=
  -- !benchmark @start postcond
  result = (v ∈ view t)
  -- !benchmark @end postcond

-- !benchmark @start lemma
theorem searchAux_correct (v : Int) :
    ∀ (t : BinarySearchTree), is_bst t → (searchAux t v = true ↔ v ∈ view t) := by
  intro t
  induction t with
  | Empty =>
      intro _
      simp [searchAux, view]
  | Node x l r ihl ihr =>
      intro h
      simp only [is_bst] at h
      obtain ⟨hl, bl, hr, br⟩ := h
      have IHl := ihl bl
      have IHr := ihr br
      simp only [searchAux, view, Set.mem_union, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
      by_cases hvx : v = x
      · simp [hvx]
      · simp only [hvx, if_false, or_false]
        by_cases hlt : v < x
        · simp only [hlt, if_true]
          rw [IHl]
          constructor
          · intro hh
            exact Or.inl hh
          · rintro (hh | hh)
            · exact hh
            · have := hr v hh
              omega
        · simp only [hlt, if_false]
          rw [IHr]
          constructor
          · intro hh
            exact Or.inr hh
          · rintro (hh | hh)
            · have := hl v hh
              omega
            · exact hh
-- !benchmark @end lemma

-- Proof content
theorem search_postcond_satisfied (t : BinarySearchTree) (v : Int)
    (h_precond : search_precond t v) :
    search_postcond t v (search t v h_precond) h_precond := by
  -- !benchmark @start proof
  have h := searchAux_correct v t h_precond
  exact propext h
  -- !benchmark @end proof

2. `searchAux` does the naive BST search: at a node with value `x`, return `true` if `v = x`, recurse left if `v < x`, else recurse right.

The student’s submission appears to satisfy the semantic requirements.

What the problem requires:
1. Implement a Binary Search Tree datatype.
2. Define/maintain the BST invariant.
3. Implement a naive BST search algorithm, i.e. compare with the node value, recurse left if smaller, right if larger.
4. Prove that search returns true iff the queried value is in the mathematical set represented by the tree view.
5. Avoid cheating tricks such as `sorry`, `admit`, empty bodies, or delegating to an existing library implementation.

What the student did:
- They defined an inductive tree type:
  - `Empty`
  - `Node : Int → BinarySearchTree → BinarySearchTree → BinarySearchTree`
- They defined a mathematical set view:
  - `view l ∪ view r ∪ {v}`
- They defined a BST invariant `is_bst`:
  - all elements in left subtree are `< v`
  - all elements in right subtree are `> v`
  - both subtrees recursively satisfy `is_bst`
- They implemented `searchAux` exactly as the standard naive BST search:
  - on empty: `false`
  - on node `x`:
    - if `v = x` return `true`
    - else if `v < x` search left
    - else search right
- The public `search` function simply calls `searchAux`, with the BST invariant as precondition.
- They provided a correctness theorem `searchAux_correct` proving
  `searchAux t v = true ↔ v ∈ view t`
  assuming `is_bst t`.
- Then they discharged the required postcondition from that theorem.

On algorithmic faithfulness:
- This is indeed the naive BST search requested in the natural language description.
- It is not replaced by a linear traversal or some library set-membership function.
- It uses the BST ordering to decide which subtree to recurse into.

On cheating / disallowed shortcuts:
- No `sorry`, `admit`, `axiom`, placeholder, or empty implementation body.
- No use of an external verified search/BST package to avoid implementing the algorithm.
- The code is self-contained apart from standard `Mathlib` imports and proof automation (`omega`), which is fine.
- The search implementation itself is explicit and genuine.

Minor note:
- The student only defines/searches on an already-formed BST via precondition `is_bst`; there is no insertion/update operation, so “maintain the invariant” is interpreted here as having and using the invariant, which is consistent with the task focus on search.

Overall, the student implemented the correct BST search algorithm from scratch and did not appear to use any trick to evade the intended task.
